```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)

set.seed(1)
```

## Functions!

Start small with Z scores.

```{r}
x_vec = rnorm(n = 40, mean = 12, sd = 63)

(x_vec - mean(x_vec)) / sd(x_vec)
```

Let's turn this into a function. This is the best methods.

```{r}
# x only exists inside this function
z_scores = function(x) {
  
  if (!is.numeric(x)){
    stop("Input x must be numeric")
  } else if (length(x) < 5) {
    stop("x should have 5 or more numbers")
  }
  
  # z only exists inside this function
  z = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
  
  return(z)
  
}
```

Does this actually work??

```{r}
z_scores(x_vec)
```

Also possible... but as a general rule, having the rule more explicit is helpful, especially when the function is longer.

```{r}
z_scores = function(x) {
  
  if (!is.numeric(x)){
    stop("Input x must be numeric")
  } else if (length(x) < 5) {
    stop("x should have 5 or more numbers")
  }
  
  z = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
  
}
```

Does this actually work??

```{r}
z_scores(x_vec)
```

Does this actually work?? Part 2

```{r}
z_scores(x_vec)
z_scores(rpois(4000, lambda = 12))

# z gets confused when you try to pass in a numeric vector or string
# z_scores(iris)
# z_scores("my name is Madeline")


# this does work (before adding if-else statement), but Jeff does not like this.
# which is why he added the if-else fn, so that it doesnt work for logical data
# types
#z_scores(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE))


# this does work (before adding if-else statement), but Jeff does not like this.
# which is why he added the if-else fn, so that it doesnt work for numerical 
# data of less than 5
# z_scores(3)
```

## Mean and sd

```{r}
mean(x_vec)
sd(x_vec)
```

Write a function that returns the mean and sd of an input vector.

```{r}
mean_and_sd = function(x) {
  
   if (!is.numeric(x)){
    stop("Input x must be numeric")
  } else if (length(x) < 5) {
    stop("x should have 5 or more numbers")
  }
  
  return_df =
    tibble(
      mean = mean(x),
      sd = sd(x)
    )
  
  return(return_df)
  
}
```

Check that this works!

```{r}
mean_and_sd(x_vec)
```

Write a function that returns the mean and sd of an input vector. Using RScript in another folder.

```{r}
source("source/mean_and_sd.R")
```

Check that this works!

```{r}
mean_and_sd(x_vec)
```

NB. Code -> "Insert Roxygen Skeleton" (in the RScript w/ function) -> Short summary of what fn is doing. See mean_and_sd.R

## Motivate and write another one!!

```{r}
sim_df =
  tibble(
    x = rnorm(n = 40, mean = 12, sd = 3)
  )

sim_df |>
  summarize(
    mean = mean(x),
    sd = sd(x)
  )
```

Small sample size and take mean you get mroe of a spread. Larger sample size and take mean you get less of a spread.

```{r}
sim_df =
  tibble(
    x = rnorm(n = 10, mean = 12, sd = 3)
  )

sim_df |>
  summarize(
    mean = mean(x),
    sd = sd(x)
  )
```

## Motivate and write another one!! Part 2

```{r}
source("source/sim_mean_sd.R")
```

Smaller mean and same sigma -> larger spread -> further away from true mean

```{r}
sim_mean_sd(n_obs = 40, mu = 12, sigma = 3)
```

Larger mean and same sigma -> smaller spread -> closer to true mean

```{r}
sim_mean_sd(n_obs = 40, mu = 150, sigma = 3)
```


```{r}
sim_mean_sd(n_obs = 40, mu = 150, sigma = 30)
```

R assumes order matches the function as defined in source file

```{r}
sim_mean_sd(40, 150, 30)
```

R assumes order matches the function as defined in source file as they move around the clearly defined argument (n_obs). When you name the arguments then you don't need them in a particular order.

```{r}
sim_mean_sd(150, n_obs = 50, 30)
```

R assumes 1st arfument and then uses the default values for the other arguments.

```{r}
sim_mean_sd(50)
```
